theme: Ordinary work as service to God
summary: Ordinary work as service to God; the dignity of all callings; the Reformation’s recovery of the sacred-secular unity
readingInstruction: Read 1 Corinthians 7:17-24 and Colossians 3:22-4:1. Today is a doctrinal pause on ordinary work as service to God, also called vocation or calling. Notice that Paul speaks to people whose jobs were not their choice, and he still says that they serve the Lord Christ.
settingTheScene: Most Christians spend most of their waking hours at work, in the home, or in the community, not in church. What does the gospel say about that? In the first century, a large portion of believers were slaves or workers in humble occupations. Paul does not tell them that real service to God is elsewhere. He tells them that their ordinary labor, done for Christ, is service to God.
observation: “Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him” (1 Corinthians 7:17).
“For he who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:22).
“You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men” (1 Corinthians 7:23).
“So, brothers, in whatever condition each was called, there let him remain with God” (1 Corinthians 7:24).
“Not with eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord” (Colossians 3:22).
“Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23).
“Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven” (Colossians 4:1).
doctrinalFocus:
The doctrine of vocation says that God calls his people not only to salvation but also to places of service in the world, and that ordinary work is a way of loving God and neighbor. The word “calling” in the New Testament primarily refers to God’s call to salvation in Christ, as in 1 Corinthians 7:17-24, where Paul speaks of the condition in which each was called. By extension, Christians have understood that God also places us in occupations, families, churches, and communities where we serve him.

During the Reformation, Martin Luther emphasized that the farmer, the mother, the magistrate, and the cobbler serve God as much as the monk or priest. Before, many believed that spiritual work was reserved for clergy. Luther said that God milks cows through the hands of milkmaids. The Reformers taught that all legitimate work is a calling, and that we serve God by serving others in it. In the Reformed tradition, this became a doctrine of the cultural mandate: from Genesis 1:28 and 2:15, human beings were made to work, tend, and cultivate the creation. Work was part of paradise; the fall made it toilsome (Genesis 3:17-19), but redemption restores its dignity.

Three truths follow. First, the Lord is the real boss. “You are serving the Lord Christ.” This gives dignity to menial jobs and removes the excuse of poor management, since our ultimate employer sees and rewards. Second, work is for others. Ephesians 4:28 says the thief should work with his hands “so that he may have something to share with anyone in need.” Work serves the neighbor and the common good. Third, our identity is not in our work. We are first called to Christ. This frees us from both pride in achievement and despair in failure.

The passage on slavery requires care. Paul is not endorsing slavery as an institution. The New Testament never commands it and regards the slave trade as sin (1 Timothy 1:10). He gives instructions to people living within it. At the same time, he undermines it: slaves are addressed as moral agents with an inheritance from the Lord, masters are told they have a Master in heaven, and in 1 Corinthians 7:21 he adds, “if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.” Philemon, which you will read soon, calls a master to receive a slave as a beloved brother. The Christian gospel, taken to its conclusion, led believers to oppose slavery.

Christians also differ on how much to emphasize staying in one’s condition (1 Corinthians 7:20, 24) versus pursuing change. Paul’s point is that your condition does not determine your standing with God, not that you can never change it.
interpretation:
In 1 Corinthians 7, Paul has been addressing marriage and singleness. He gives a general rule: “Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him. This is my rule in all the churches.” Circumcised or uncircumcised, it does not matter; keeping God’s commandments is what matters. “Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called.” Were you a slave when called? “Do not be concerned about it. (But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.) For he who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord. Likewise he who was free when called is a bondservant of Christ. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men.” The gospel gives a new status that cannot be taken away. A slave is the Lord’s freedman; a free person is Christ’s slave. The social ranking is secondary.

In Colossians 3, Paul turns to practical conduct. “Bondservants, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters, not with eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord.” Eye-service is working only when the boss is watching. “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ.” The slave had no legal rights, but Paul tells him that he has an inheritance, which the free would normally receive. The reward is not wages but the inheritance of the sons of God. In a world where slaves were considered tools, this was radical.

The principle applies to every honest job. Whatever you do, do it heartily. The Christian employee, student, parent, teacher, cleaner, or executive works for a higher Lord. This changes how we work (with diligence), why we work (for his glory and others’ good), and how we rest (in his provision). Mundane tasks are holy when done to the Lord.
connection: Genesis 1:28 and 2:15 give the work mandate. Genesis 3:17-19 describes the toil after the fall. Exodus 31:1-6 describes the Spirit-filled craftsmen. Proverbs 6:6-11 and 22:29 praise diligent work. Ephesians 4:28 and 6:5-9 speak of work and slaves. 2 Thessalonians 3:6-12 warns against idleness. 1 Corinthians 10:31 says do all to the glory of God. Philemon is the test case. Psalm 90:17 prays for the work of our hands to be established. Matthew 25:14-30 teaches faithfulness in what we have been given.
application:
Do your next task today as if Christ were your employer. Notice what changes.

Thank God for the occupation he has given you, even if it’s imperfect.

Think about someone whose work is invisible, like a janitor or a caregiver. Honor them this week.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the work he has given you, and tell him what it is.
Ask him to help you work heartily, as for the Lord.
Ask him to show you how your ordinary work can serve him and others.
